title: Finite exceptional-curve data for a normal excellent surface modification
statement:
Let $X$ be a normal integral excellent Noetherian scheme of topological dimension $2$, where excellence is required on every affine coordinate ring [def-pc-integral-scheme, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring, def-exc-excellent-ring, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Let $f:Y	o X$ be proper with $Y$ integral and with $k(X)	o k(Y)$ an isomorphism [def-weil-proper-morphism, def-sc-function-field]. Let $
u:Z=Y^
u	o Y$ be normalization in $k(Y)$ [def-sc-normalization], and put $h=f
u$. Then $
u$ is finite and proper, $Z$ is normal integral excellent Noetherian of dimension $2$, and $h$ is proper and induces an isomorphism of function fields [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. If $Y$ is already normal, $
u$ is an isomorphism. Define $B(h)$ to be the set of integral closed subschemes $C\subset Z$ of topological dimension $1$ whose image under $h$ is one point; integral closed subsets always carry the reduced induced scheme structure [def-weil-closed-immersion]. The set $B(h)$ is finite; every contraction point $x=h(C)$ is closed in $X$; and $h$ is an isomorphism if and only if $B(h)$ is empty. For every $C\in B(h)$ with generic point $\eta_C$ [def-sc-generic-point], the local ring $R_C=\mathcal O_{Z,\eta_C}\subset k(Z)$ is a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]; the induced map $\mathcal O_{X,x}	o R_C$ is local and injective, with common fraction field $k(X)=k(Z)$; and $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(x)}\kappa(\eta_C)=1$ [def-weil-residue-field, def-kun-transcendence-degree].

source.place: Tag 0BBT (resolve-lemma-dominate-by-normalized-blowing-up), proof first two paragraphs, normalization reduction and finiteness/base case for BadCurves; the generic DVR and residue-field observations in the fourth paragraph. Supporting Tags 0BFP (varieties-lemma-modification-normal-iso-over-codimension-1), 0A21(6) (varieties-lemma-dimension-locally-algebraic), and 00PD (algebra-lemma-characterize-dvr). The first paragraph uses finite-type stability of excellence and finite normalization, not resolution.

proof.text: Properness makes $f$ finite type. The finite-type-over-Noetherian theorem makes $Y$ Noetherian. On each affine chart over an affine of $X$, its coordinate ring is a finite type algebra over an excellent ring, hence excellent by the finite-type excellence theorem (take the multiplicative set $\{1\}$). The affine-cover criterion then gives excellence on every affine open of $Y$.

source.place: Tag 0BBT, lemma-dominate-by-normalized-blowing-up, first proof paragraph; supporting Tags 01T6, 07QU, 0HAB

proof.text: Since $Y$ is integral it is reduced and has just one irreducible component, itself. Thus its componentwise normalization is exactly its function-field normalization $\nu:Z\to Y$. The excellent normalization preparation theorem gives finiteness and surjectivity of $\nu$, and normality, Noetherianity and excellence of $Z$.

source.place: Tag 0BBT, first proof paragraph; Tags 035S and 035Q

proof.text: The affine normalization charts are $\operatorname{Spec}\overline A$, where $A$ is a domain and $A\subseteq\overline A\subseteq\operatorname{Frac}(A)=k(Y)$. Consequently $\overline A$ is a domain with fraction field $k(Y)$: the inclusions give both inclusions of fraction fields. The generic points of these charts agree on their nonempty overlaps, since they all map to the generic point of $Y$ and have the same fraction-field chart. Hence $Z$ is integral and $k(Y)\to k(Z)$ is an isomorphism. Composing with the given isomorphism gives $k(X)=k(Z)$.

Finite morphisms are proper, so $
u$ is proper; composition makes $h=f
u$ proper. In particular it is finite type and closed. Its generic point maps to the generic point of $X$, so it is dominant. The closed dominant dimension formula, with the function-field extension of transcendence degree zero, gives $\dim Z=\dim X=2$. If $Y$ was already normal, apply the finite birational normal-target isomorphism theorem to $
u$ to conclude that $
u$ is an isomorphism.

We will use the following elementary interpretation of local dimension on $X$ and $Z$. At a point $s$ choose an affine neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}A$, with corresponding prime $\mathfrak p$. The stalk is $A_{\mathfrak p}$; its primes correspond, preserving strict inclusions in both directions, to primes of $A$ contained in $\mathfrak p$. These correspond to generizations of $s$ (specialization in an affine spectrum is inclusion of primes). All generizations lie in every open neighbourhood of $s$. Taking closures in the whole scheme therefore identifies their strict chains with chains of irreducible closed subsets ending at $\overline{\{s\}}$. Thus $\dim\mathcal O_{S,s}$ is the supremum of lengths of these chains. On an integral scheme such chains can start at the generic point; on our surfaces their lengths are at most $2$.

source.place: Tag 01J7, lemma-specialize-points; affine verification using algebra Tag 00E3, lemma-spec-localization

proof.text: The stalks of $X$ and $Z$ are Noetherian: use their Noetherian affine covers, the affine-stalk localization isomorphism, and preservation of Noetherianity under localization. They are normal local domains by normality of the schemes. At any point of local dimension one, the one-dimensional normal local domain theorem therefore says the stalk is a DVR.

source.place: Tag 00PD, lemma-characterize-dvr, equivalence (5) with (1); localization Noetherianity

proof.text: Apply the normal modification theorem to $h:Z\to X$. Its hypotheses hold: $X$ is Noetherian, $Z$ is integral hence reduced, $h$ is proper, and its generic local-ring map is the function-field isomorphism, so it is birational in the theorem's stated sense. Let $U$ be the maximal open where $h$ is an isomorphism, and $T=X\setminus U$. Clauses (1) and (2), together with the DVR conclusion of step 6, show that every point of $T$ has local dimension $2$. Clause (3) will also show that any point with a finite fibre belongs to $U$, since every local ring of $X$ is normal.

Every point $t\in T$ is closed: a proper specialization of $t$ would append one term to a length-two generization chain ending at $t$ (step 5), giving a chain of length three in $X$, contrary to $\dim X=2$. The closed subset $T$ has finitely many irreducible components by the Noetherian closed-subset component theorem. Each component has a generic point, and that point is closed by the preceding argument; hence the component is a singleton. Thus $T$ is a finite set of closed points. This includes $T=\varnothing$.

source.place: Tag 0BBT, second proof paragraph: finite closed exceptional set; supporting Tag 0BA8

proof.text: If $C\in B(h)$ and $h(C)=\{x\}$, properness of $h$ implies that $\{x\}$ is closed, since $C$ is closed and a proper map is closed. Moreover $x\notin U$: otherwise the isomorphism $h^{-1}U\simeq U$ would identify the underlying space of $C$ with the singleton $\{x\}$, contradicting $\dim C=1$. Therefore every contracted curve lies over one of the finitely many points of $T$.

source.place: Tag 0BBT, second proof paragraph, identification of BadCurves with curves above the exceptional points

proof.text: For each $x\in T$, the closed subset $F_x=h^{-1}(\{x\})$ is proper in $Z$, because the generic point of $Z$ maps to the generic point of $X$, not to $x$. Every irreducible closed subset of $F_x$ has dimension at most one: adjoining $Z$ to any of its chains adds one strict inclusion in the two-dimensional integral space $Z$. It has finitely many irreducible components by the Noetherian closed-subset component theorem. A one-dimensional irreducible closed subset $C\subseteq F_x$ must itself be a component: if $C\subsetneq D$ for an irreducible component $D$ of $F_x$, a length-one chain in $C$ followed by $D$ would give $\dim D\geq2$. Conversely every one-dimensional component, endowed with its reduced induced closed scheme structure, is a member of $B(h)$. Thus $B(h)$ is a subset of a finite union of finite component sets, and is finite.

source.place: Tag 0BBT, second proof paragraph, finiteness of BadCurves; no connectedness or purity of the fibres is needed

proof.text: If $B(h)=\varnothing$, every irreducible component of each $F_x$, $x\in T$, has dimension zero by step 10. Such a component is a singleton: its generic point exists, and a distinct point would give a nontrivial specialization and hence a length-one chain. The finitely many components therefore make $F_x$ finite. Clause (3) of the normal modification theorem now forces $x\in U$, a contradiction. Hence $T=\varnothing$ and $h$ is an isomorphism. Conversely an isomorphism cannot contract a one-dimensional closed subset to a singleton, so $h$ an isomorphism implies $B(h)=\varnothing$.

source.place: Tag 0BBT, second proof paragraph, base case; Tag 0BFP, clause (3)

proof.text: Fix $C\in B(h)$ and put $\eta=\eta_C$. Its local dimension on $Z$ is one. Indeed $\eta$ differs from the generic point of $Z$, so it has a strict generization and local dimension at least one. If its local dimension were at least two, a length-two chain ending at $C=\overline{\{\eta\}}$, followed by a proper nonempty irreducible closed subset of the one-dimensional $C$, would give a length-three chain in $Z$. This is impossible. Apply step 6, or directly the one-dimensional Noetherian normal local domain theorem, to obtain that $R_C=\mathcal O_{Z,\eta}$ is a DVR.

source.place: Tag 0BBT, fourth proof paragraph, use of ord at the generic point of a bad curve; algebra Tag 00PD (5)

proof.text: Set $x=h(\eta)=h(C)$. The stalk map $\mathcal O_{X,x}\to\mathcal O_{Z,\eta}$ is local by the definition of a scheme morphism. Both rings embed in their function fields: on an integral affine chart the section ring embeds in the generic stalk, and its localization at any prime embeds in the same field by $a/s\mapsto a/s$. The fraction field of that localization is still the fraction field of the section ring, since it contains the section ring. The stalk map commutes with the maps to the generic stalks, by restriction of the structure-sheaf morphism. Under $k(X)=k(Z)$ its composite with $R_C\hookrightarrow k(Z)$ is the inclusion $\mathcal O_{X,x}\hookrightarrow k(X)$, so it is injective and both fraction fields are this common field.

source.place: Tag 0BBT, fourth proof paragraph, common fraction fields; supporting Tags 01RV and 01HV

proof.text: Finally take the scheme-theoretic fibre $Z_x=Z\times_X\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$. It is finite type over $\kappa(x)$ by finite-type base change. The fibre's underlying space is homeomorphic to $F_x$, so the closed irreducible subset $C$ corresponds to a one-dimensional closed irreducible subset of $Z_x$, with corresponding generic point $\widetilde\eta$. The dimension/transcendence-degree theorem over a field gives $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(x)}\kappa_{Z_x}(\widetilde\eta)=1$. Its residue field is canonically $\kappa_Z(\eta)$ as a $\kappa(x)$-field: on affine charts this is exactly the fibre-ring primes/residue-fields theorem for $B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and the prime of $B$ corresponding to $\eta$. Thus $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(x)}\kappa(\eta_C)=1$, as required.
